name: Neon tetra
notes: A small schooling tetra with a bright blue and red stripe. Looks best in a group of eight or more in a planted tank.

name: Cardinal tetra
notes: Like a neon tetra with red running the full length of the body. Prefers soft, slightly acidic water and warmer temperatures.

name: Ember tetra
notes: A tiny orange tetra that suits nano tanks. Easily eaten by larger fish, so keep it with other small, peaceful species.

name: Black skirt tetra
notes: Hardy and active. Can nip the fins of slow, long-finned fish, especially when kept in small groups.

name: Serpae tetra
notes: A red tetra known for fin nipping. A larger group spreads the nipping among its own kind.

name: Rummynose tetra
notes: Schools tightly, with a red nose that fades when water quality drops, which makes it a useful early warning.

name: Glowlight tetra
notes: A calm tetra with a glowing orange line. A good alternative to neons for beginners.

name: Lemon tetra
notes: A pale yellow tetra with black and yellow fin edges. Colors improve with a varied diet.

name: Harlequin rasbora
notes: Copper body with a black triangle patch. One of the easiest schooling fish for a community tank.

name: Chili rasbora
notes: One of the smallest aquarium fish. Best in a quiet planted nano tank without larger tankmates.

name: Celestial pearl danio
notes: Also sold as galaxy rasbora. Shy at first, so dense plants help it settle and show color.

name: Zebra danio
notes: Fast, tough and always moving. A longer tank gives it room to swim.

name: White cloud mountain minnow
notes: A cool-water fish that does well without a heater in a room-temperature tank.

name: Cherry barb
notes: One of the few peaceful barbs. Males turn deep red when kept with females.

name: Tiger barb
notes: Bold and playful but a well known fin nipper. Keep in groups of six or more and away from slow, long-finned fish.

name: Guppy
notes: Colorful livebearer that breeds readily. Keep more females than males, or an all-male group.

name: Endler's livebearer
notes: A smaller, hardier relative of the guppy. Breeds quickly, so plan for fry.

name: Platy
notes: Hardy, colorful and forgiving. A classic first fish for hard tap water.

name: Molly
notes: Needs hard, alkaline water. Grows larger than most people expect and produces a lot of waste.

name: Swordtail
notes: Males carry a long sword on the tail and can squabble with each other. Keep one male with several females.

name: Betta (male)
notes: Male bettas fight each other and must be kept alone or with calm, short-finned tankmates.

name: Honey gourami
notes: The gentlest gourami. A good centerpiece for a small community tank.

name: Dwarf gourami
notes: Bright and calm with other species, but males fight each other. Buy from a trusted source, as the species is prone to disease.

name: Pearl gourami
notes: A large, graceful gourami covered in pearl-like spots. Peaceful enough for most community tanks.

name: Angelfish
notes: Elegant and tall, so it needs a tall tank. Adults will eat very small fish such as neon tetras.

name: Discus
notes: Needs very warm, clean, soft water and frequent water changes. Best for experienced keepers.

name: German blue ram
notes: A colorful dwarf cichlid that needs warm, soft, very clean water.

name: Bolivian ram
notes: Hardier than the German blue ram and calm in community tanks.

name: Kribensis
notes: A small cichlid that becomes protective when breeding. Give it caves and space.

name: Cockatoo dwarf cichlid
notes: Males show a tall, spiky dorsal fin. Each one claims a cave, so give one per fish.

name: Convict cichlid
notes: Tough and easy to breed, but very aggressive when guarding eggs.

name: Oscar
notes: A large, intelligent cichlid with a big appetite. It will eat any fish that fits in its mouth.

name: Bronze corydoras
notes: A hardy catfish that sifts the sand in busy groups. Use smooth sand to protect its barbels.

name: Panda corydoras
notes: A small cory with panda-like eye patches. Prefers slightly cooler water than most corys.

name: Sterbai corydoras
notes: Tolerates warmer water than most corys, so it pairs well with rams and discus.

name: Pygmy corydoras
notes: A tiny cory that often swims in mid-water schools instead of staying on the bottom.

name: Bristlenose pleco
notes: The best pleco for most home tanks. Needs driftwood to graze and produces a lot of waste.

name: Otocinclus
notes: A small algae eater that needs a mature tank with plenty of soft algae to graze.

name: Kuhli loach
notes: An eel-like loach that hides by day. In a group with soft sand, it comes out much more.

name: Clown loach
notes: Sold small but grows to a foot long over many years. Needs a large tank and a group.

name: Siamese algae eater
notes: Eats many kinds of algae, including black beard algae. Grows large and can jump, so use a lid.

name: Rainbow shark
notes: Claims the bottom of the tank and chases similar fish. Keep only one.

name: Bala shark
notes: A fast, peaceful schooler that gets very large. Adults will eat small fish.

name: Common goldfish
notes: Grows much larger than people expect and is best suited to ponds or very large tanks.

name: Fancy goldfish
notes: Slow-swimming goldfish with rounded bodies. Keep with other fancies, not with fast tropical fish.
